titre: The Piano Owes Its Name to What the Harpsichord Could Not Do
accroche: A harpsichord always plays at the same intensity, whether you strike the key hard or softly. Around 1700, a Florentine maker solves the problem.
contenu_vulgarise:
Since the 16th century, the harpsichord has been the reference keyboard instrument in Europe. Each key activates a small quill plectrum that plucks a string: the force of the finger changes nothing about the intensity of the sound, only its presence or absence. A harpsichordist can vary touch, tempo, articulation, but not volume note by note. The harpsichord knows neither crescendo nor dynamics.

In 1688, Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument maker born in Padua, enters the service of Prince Ferdinando de' Medici in Florence as keeper of the musical instruments. Between that date and 1700, he develops an entirely different mechanism: instead of plucking the string, a hammer strikes it. The 1700 inventory of the Medici court already describes an “arpicembalo che fa' il piano, e il forte,” a harp-harpsichord that makes the soft and the loud.

## A spring, not a hammer that stays stuck

The technical difficulty is not making a hammer strike a string: it is pulling it away right afterward, without which it would smother the sound it has just produced. For this, Cristofori designs an escapement mechanism: a spring-loaded piece, housed in the key, pushes the hammer toward the string and then disengages by itself just before impact, letting the hammer finish its travel alone and fall straight back into a device that keeps it from bouncing on the string. Because the speed of the hammer depends directly on the force applied to the key, and not on a plucking of fixed strength, the instrument finally responds to touch: pressing hard gives a loud sound, pressing softly gives a soft one.

In 1711, the Veronese scholar Scipione Maffei publishes, in the *Giornale de' letterati d'Italia*, the first detailed description of this mechanism, accompanied by an engraving of the action, and mistakenly spells the inventor's name “Cristofali.” It is this publication, translated into German in 1725, that makes the invention known outside Italy; locally, some harpsichordists then find it too muffled, too dull next to the brilliance of the harpsichord.

## What it shifts

The name that remains, pianoforte, then simply piano, describes nothing other than this precise defect of the harpsichord, corrected: playing soft or loud at will. It is not an instrument name like violin or trumpet, which designates a shape; it is the name of a problem solved. Only a handful of Cristofori pianos survive today, including an example from 1720 kept at the Metropolitan Museum in New York, largely modified since: the oldest material trace of a gesture that every pianist still repeats, that of varying the sound under the fingers.

repere.texte: In 1700, the inventory of the Medici court in Florence already mentions an “arpicembalo che fa' il piano, e il forte.” In 1711, Scipione Maffei publishes in the Giornale de' letterati d'Italia the first detailed description of the mechanism, with an engraving of the action in support.

carte.punch: No matter how hard you press, a harpsichord can't play louder. Around 1700, a maker fixes that.
carte.idee: The harpsichord always plucks its strings with the same force: impossible to shade a sound. Around 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori invents a hammer-and-escapement mechanism in which the speed of the blow depends on the force of the finger. Its name, pianoforte, describes only that corrected defect.

quiz.question: Why does Cristofori's mechanism make it possible to play soft or loud, unlike the harpsichord?
choix: Because its strings are longer and therefore vibrate louder once plucked
Because a hammer strikes the string with a force proportional to the one applied to the key
Because a special pedal adjusts the overall volume of the whole instrument
Because the wooden case amplifies the sound differently depending on playing speed
quiz.explication: The harpsichord plucks its strings with a fixed force, whatever the speed of the finger: the volume therefore never varies. Cristofori's mechanism replaces the plucking with a hammer whose speed depends directly on the force applied to the key, which finally makes it possible to shade the sound while playing. Neither the length of the strings, nor a pedal, nor the case is the cause: the change lies entirely in the action of the hammer.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and by whom does Cristofori enter the service of the court where he invents his mechanism?
choix: In 1688, in the service of Prince Ferdinando de' Medici in Florence, as keeper of the musical instruments
In 1700, in the service of the King of France, as official maker of the court's harpsichords
In 1711, in the service of Scipione Maffei, as a research assistant
In 1725, in the service of the Viennese court, as a music teacher
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cristofori enters in 1688 the service of Prince Ferdinando de' Medici in Florence as keeper of the musical instruments, a post he holds when he develops his mechanism between that date and 1700.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What mistake does Scipione Maffei make in publishing, in 1711, the first detailed description of the mechanism?
choix: He dates the invention ten years too early
He misspells the inventor's name, writing Cristofali
He attributes the invention to a Venetian maker rather than a Florentine one
He omits the escapement mechanism from his engraving
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Maffei publishes in 1711 the first detailed description of the mechanism, but mistakenly spells the name of the inventor Cristofori as Cristofali, an error later repeated in several texts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did harpsichordists of the day first receive Cristofori's instrument, once the invention was known outside Italy?
choix: They adopted it immediately in all the royal orchestras
They accused it of copying an instrument already invented in Germany
They judged it too muffled and too dull next to the brilliance of the harpsichord
They refused to see it as anything but a toy for children
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Once the invention was known in Europe through the 1725 German translation, some harpsichordists found the new instrument too muffled and too dull compared with the brighter sound of the harpsichord.
